name: slap tear
aliases: superior labrum anterior to posterior lesion

clinicalPearls: A SLAP lesion is an injury to the superior labrum extending anterior to posterior around the biceps anchor at the supraglenoid tubercle.
Two dominant mechanisms are recognised: a fall onto an outstretched or abducted arm (compression), and repetitive overhead throwing generating a peel-back force on the biceps-labral complex.
The Snyder classification describes four principal types, ranging from fraying to bucket-handle detachment with biceps anchor involvement and extension into adjacent labrum.
Symptoms are often vague deep-seated pain, clicking or catching, and loss of throwing velocity, making clinical diagnosis difficult.
Provocative tests such as O'Brien active compression, the biceps load and dynamic labral shear tests aid diagnosis but individually lack accuracy, so combine several.
A key mimic and normal variant is the sublabral foramen and Buford complex; misinterpreting these leads to overdiagnosis.
In older patients an incidental degenerate superior labral change is common and repairing it may worsen stiffness, so treat the symptomatic lesion, not the image.

Biceps tenodesis or tenotomy is often preferred over labral repair in older patients and those with biceps pathology, whereas anatomical repair suits younger overhead athletes with true unstable lesions.
reference.pathophysiology: The superior labrum anchors the long head of biceps tendon at the supraglenoid tubercle and contributes to glenohumeral stability by deepening the socket. SLAP lesions arise when this biceps-labral complex is disrupted, either by an acute traction or compression load or by repetitive microtrauma. In overhead throwers, the late cocking position generates a posterosuperior peel-back force that progressively strips the superior labrum from the glenoid; associated posterior capsular tightness and glenohumeral internal rotation deficit shift the contact point and amplify this stress. Acute injuries typically follow a fall on an outstretched arm or a sudden traction event. An unstable superior labrum destabilises the biceps anchor, alters humeral head kinematics and can produce pseudolaxity, pain and mechanical symptoms; with time degenerative fraying accumulates independently of a discrete injury.
additionalDifferentials: Internal (posterosuperior) impingement in the overhead athlete
Biceps tendinopathy or instability of the long head
Normal labral variants (sublabral foramen, Buford complex)
Paralabral cyst causing suprascapular nerve compression
additionalInvestigations: MR arthrography, the most accurate imaging for superior labral pathology
Standard MRI to assess the cuff, biceps and any paralabral cyst
Plain radiographs to exclude bony and degenerative causes
Diagnostic arthroscopy for direct assessment and dynamic peel-back testing
Assessment for glenohumeral internal rotation deficit and posterior capsular tightness
Electrophysiological studies if suprascapular neuropathy from a paralabral cyst is suspected
redFlags: Associated large rotator cuff tear with significant weakness
Features of a paralabral cyst compressing the suprascapular nerve with infraspinatus wasting
Mechanical locking suggesting a displaced bucket-handle labral fragment
Coexisting instability with recurrent subluxation or dislocation
reference.prognosis: Younger overhead athletes with a true unstable lesion can achieve good pain relief with repair, though return to the previous level of throwing is less predictable. In older patients and those with degenerative changes, biceps tenodesis or tenotomy generally provides more reliable relief than labral repair.
pitfalls: Overdiagnosing a SLAP tear by mistaking normal labral variants for pathology.
Repairing a degenerate superior labrum in an older patient and precipitating stiffness.
Relying on a single provocative test given their limited individual accuracy.
Failing to address associated internal impingement, cuff pathology or a paralabral cyst.
references: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Trauma
management: Start with non-operative management using physiotherapy that strengthens the scapular stabilisers and rotator cuff and restores internal rotation, with posterior capsular stretching
Provide activity modification, analgesia and a selective corticosteroid injection
Perform arthroscopic repair of a true unstable superior labral tear in younger overhead athletes
Prefer biceps tenodesis or tenotomy for older patients and those with degenerative labral change, as these give more reliable relief
Treat associated lesions and decompress a symptomatic paralabral cyst causing suprascapular neuropathy
Avoid over-treatment of normal variants such as the sublabral foramen and Buford complex
Progress rehabilitation with a staged return to throwing
